title: UNIT 6: ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES AND GEOMETRICAL OPTICS
notes: ✓ Electromagnetic waves and geometrical optics → Study electromagnetic waves, the electromagnetic spectrum, light, reflection, refraction, mirrors, lenses, the human eye, optical instruments and color.

title: 6.1 ELECTROMAGNETIC (EM) WAVES
notes:
✓ Electromagnetic wave → Wave consisting of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that propagate outward from a source.

✓ EM waves → Are produced by accelerating/vibrating charged particles.

◆ CHARACTERISTICS
✓ Electric and magnetic fields → Oscillate at right angles to each other.
✓ Both fields → Are perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
✓ EM waves → Are transverse waves.
✓ EM waves → Can travel through empty space/vacuum.
✓ EM waves → Can also travel through matter.
✓ EM waves → Transfer energy without transferring matter.

◆ MECHANICAL vs EM WAVES
✓ Mechanical waves → Require a material medium.
✓ EM waves → Can propagate through a vacuum.

◆ WAVELENGTH (λ)
✓ Wavelength → Distance between successive corresponding points such as crests.

◆ FREQUENCY (f)
✓ Frequency → Number of oscillations per second; unit Hz.

◆ RADIANT ENERGY
✓ Radiant energy → Energy carried by EM waves.
✓ Sun → Sends radiant energy to Earth mainly through infrared and visible light, with a smaller amount carried through ultraviolet radiation.

✓ KEY IDEA → EM waves carry energy and do not require a material medium for propagation.

title: 6.2 ELECTROMAGNETIC SPECTRUM
notes:
✓ Electromagnetic spectrum → Complete range of electromagnetic radiation arranged according to frequency or wavelength.

✓ Long wavelength → Low frequency → Low energy.
✓ Short wavelength → High frequency → High energy.

◆ MAIN REGIONS
✓ Radio → Microwaves → Infrared → Visible → Ultraviolet → X-rays → Gamma rays.

✓ All are EM waves → They differ mainly in wavelength, frequency and energy.

title: 6.2 RADIO WAVES & MICROWAVES
notes:
◆ RADIO WAVES
✓ Radio waves → Have the longest wavelengths and lowest frequencies in the EM spectrum.

◆ USES
Radio communication.
Television transmission.
Police and military communication.
Communication systems.

✓ Excessive exposure to intense radio-frequency radiation → Can be harmful.

◆ MICROWAVES
✓ Microwaves → Are high-frequency radio waves with shorter wavelengths than ordinary radio waves.

◆ USES
Microwave ovens.
Mobile communication.
Radar.
Aircraft and ship navigation.
Weather forecasting.
Traffic speed detection.

✓ Strong microwave exposure → Can heat body tissues and may damage sensitive tissues such as the eyes.

title: 6.2 INFRARED & VISIBLE LIGHT
notes:
◆ INFRARED (IR)
✓ Infrared radiation → Lies just beyond the red end of visible light.

◆ SOURCES
✓ Hot objects, stars, lamps, flames and other warm bodies → Emit infrared radiation.

◆ USES
TV and video remote controls.
Heat lamps.
Physiotherapy.
Thermal applications.

◆ VISIBLE LIGHT
✓ Visible light → Part of the EM spectrum that can be detected by the human eye.
✓ Visible light → Enables human vision and is emitted by sources such as the Sun and lamps.

✓ KEY IDEA → Infrared is mainly associated with thermal radiation, while visible light is the region detected by the human eye.

title: 6.2 ULTRAVIOLET, X-RAYS & GAMMA RAYS
notes:
◆ ULTRAVIOLET (UV)
✓ UV → Has higher frequency and energy than visible light.

◆ USES
Sterilization • some medical applications • detection/analysis.

✓ Excessive UV exposure → Can damage skin and eyes and cause sunburn.

◆ X-RAYS
✓ X-rays → Have very high frequency and penetrating ability.

◆ USES
Medical imaging.
Airport/security inspection.
Astronomical observations.

✓ Excessive X-ray exposure → Can damage cells and increase cancer risk, so shielding is used.

◆ GAMMA RAYS
✓ Gamma rays → Have the highest frequencies and energies in the spectrum and are highly penetrating.

◆ USES
Cancer treatment/radiotherapy.
Sterilizing medical equipment.
Food irradiation.
Industrial tracers.

✓ Gamma radiation → Can damage living cells, cause mutations and increase cancer risk.

✓ SPECTRUM TREND → Frequency ↑ → Energy ↑ → Wavelength ↓.

title: 6.3 LIGHT AS A WAVE
notes:
✓ Light → Form of electromagnetic wave that carries energy.
✓ Visible light → Portion of the EM spectrum detectable by humans.

◆ MEDIUM OF PROPAGATION
✓ Light → Can travel through transparent materials such as air, water and glass.
✓ Light → Does not require matter and can travel through a vacuum.

◆ SPEED OF LIGHT
✓ In vacuum:
c = 2.99792458 × 10⁸ m/s ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s

✓ For EM waves:
c = fλ

✓ c → Speed.
✓ f → Frequency.
✓ λ → Wavelength.

✓ KEY IDEA → In vacuum, EM waves travel at the same speed regardless of their frequency; their wavelengths change when their frequencies differ.

title: 6.4 LAWS OF REFLECTION
notes:
✓ Reflection → Bouncing back of light when it strikes a surface.

◆ IMPORTANT TERMS
✓ Incident ray → Incoming light ray.
✓ Reflected ray → Ray leaving the surface.
✓ Normal → Imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.
✓ Angle of incidence (i) → Angle between incident ray and normal.
✓ Angle of reflection (r) → Angle between reflected ray and normal.

◆ LAWS OF REFLECTION
✓ Angle of incidence = angle of reflection:
i = r

✓ Incident ray, reflected ray and normal → Lie in the same plane.

◆ SPECULAR REFLECTION
✓ Specular reflection → Occurs on a smooth surface; parallel incident rays remain parallel after reflection.

◆ DIFFUSE REFLECTION
✓ Diffuse reflection → Occurs on a rough surface; parallel incident rays are reflected in different directions.

✓ KEY IDEA → Angles of reflection are measured from the normal, not from the surface.

title: 6.4 REFRACTION OF LIGHT
notes:
✓ Refraction → Bending/change in direction of light when it passes from one transparent medium into another because its speed changes.

◆ REFRACTION BEHAVIOR
✓ Light enters a medium where it travels more slowly → Bends toward the normal.
✓ Light enters a medium where it travels faster → Bends away from the normal.

◆ REFRACTIVE INDEX
n = c/v

✓ c → Speed of light in vacuum.
✓ v → Speed of light in the medium.

◆ SNELL'S LAW
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂

✓ θ₁ and θ₂ → Are measured from the normal.

◆ IMPORTANT
✓ Light enters a different medium → Its speed and wavelength change, but its frequency remains unchanged.

✓ KEY IDEA → Refraction occurs because light travels at different speeds in different media.

title: 6.4 TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION & DISPERSION
notes:
◆ TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION
✓ Total internal reflection → Occurs when light travels from a denser medium to a less dense medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.

◆ CONDITIONS
✓ Light → Travels from higher refractive index to lower refractive index.
✓ Angle of incidence → Greater than critical angle.

◆ DISPERSION
✓ Dispersion → Separation of white light into its component colors because different wavelengths are refracted by different amounts.

✓ Visible spectrum → Red → Orange → Yellow → Green → Blue → Indigo → Violet.

◆ RAINBOW
✓ Rainbow → Forms through refraction, dispersion and internal reflection of sunlight in water droplets.

✓ KEY IDEA → Violet is deviated more than red in ordinary glass.

title: 6.5 MIRRORS
notes:
✓ Mirror → Reflecting surface that forms images through reflection.

◆ PLANE MIRROR
✓ Image → Virtual.
✓ Image → Upright/erect.
✓ Image → Same size as the object.
✓ Image → Laterally inverted.
✓ Image → Same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.

◆ CONCAVE MIRROR
✓ Concave mirror → Converging mirror whose reflecting surface curves inward.
✓ Concave mirror → Can produce real or virtual images depending on object position.

◆ CONVEX MIRROR
✓ Convex mirror → Diverging mirror whose reflecting surface curves outward.
✓ Convex mirror → Always forms a virtual, upright and diminished image for a real object.

◆ MIRROR EQUATION
1/f = 1/u + 1/v

✓ Magnification:
m = hᵢ/hₒ = −v/u

✓ f → Focal length.
✓ u → Object distance.
✓ v → Image distance.

✓ KEY IDEA → Concave mirrors can magnify or form real images; convex mirrors provide a wide field of view.

title: 6.5 RAY DIAGRAMS FOR CONCAVE MIRRORS
notes:
◆ IMPORTANT POINTS
✓ O → Pole of mirror.
✓ F → Principal focus.
✓ C → Center of curvature.

✓ For a spherical mirror:
f = R/2

✓ R → Radius of curvature.

◆ PRINCIPAL RAYS
✓ Ray parallel to principal axis → Reflects through F for a concave mirror.
✓ Ray through F → Reflects parallel to the principal axis.
✓ Ray through C → Is reflected back along its original path.

✓ Intersection of reflected rays → Determines the image position.

✓ KEY IMAGE TYPE → Depends on the position of the object relative to F and C.

title: LENSES
notes:
✓ Lens → Transparent optical element that refracts light.

◆ CONVEX LENS
✓ Convex lens → Converging lens that is thicker at the center than at the edges.
✓ Parallel rays → Converge toward the principal focus.

◆ CONCAVE LENS
✓ Concave lens → Diverging lens that is thinner at the center than at the edges.
✓ Parallel rays → Diverge as if they came from the principal focus.

◆ THIN-LENS EQUATION
1/f = 1/u + 1/v

◆ MAGNIFICATION
m = hᵢ/hₒ = v/u

✓ f → Focal length.
✓ u → Object distance.
✓ v → Image distance.

✓ KEY IDEA
✓ Convex lens → Converging.
✓ Concave lens → Diverging.

title: 6.5 IMAGE FORMATION BY LENSES
notes:
◆ CONVEX LENS
✓ Object beyond 2F → Real, inverted and diminished image between F and 2F.
✓ Object at 2F → Real, inverted and same-size image at 2F.
✓ Object between F and 2F → Real, inverted and enlarged image beyond 2F.
✓ Object at F → Image forms effectively at infinity.
✓ Object between F and optical center → Virtual, upright and enlarged image.

◆ CONCAVE LENS
✓ For a real object, a concave lens → Forms a virtual, upright and diminished image.

◆ LENS POWER
P = 1/f

✓ f → Measured in metres.
✓ Unit → Dioptre (D).

✓ KEY IDEA → The position of the object determines the size, orientation and nature of the image.

title: 6.6 HUMAN EYE
notes:
✓ Human eye → Functions like an optical camera; its lens system forms an image on the light-sensitive retina.

◆ CORNEA
✓ Cornea → Transparent front surface; much of the initial refraction occurs here.

◆ IRIS
✓ Iris → Muscular diaphragm controlling pupil size.

◆ PUPIL
✓ Pupil → Opening through which light enters.

◆ CRYSTALLINE LENS
✓ Crystalline lens → Provides fine adjustment of focal length.

◆ CILIARY MUSCLES
✓ Ciliary muscles → Change the shape/focusing power of the eye lens.

◆ RETINA
✓ Retina → Light-sensitive layer where the image is formed.

◆ IMAGE ON RETINA
✓ Eye → Forms a real and inverted image on the retina.

◆ ACCOMMODATION
✓ Accommodation → Ability of the eye lens to change its focal length so that objects at different distances can be focused on the retina.

◆ NORMAL NEAR POINT
✓ Approximately 25 cm → Normal near point for a normal eye.

✓ KEY IDEA → The cornea and lens focus incoming light onto the retina.

title: 6.6 DEFECTS OF VISION
notes:
◆ MYOPIA (SHORT-SIGHTEDNESS)
✓ Myopia → Distant objects are not focused correctly on the retina; the image tends to form in front of the retina.
✓ Correction → Concave/diverging lens.

◆ HYPERMETROPIA (LONG-SIGHTEDNESS)
✓ Hypermetropia → Nearby objects are not focused correctly; the image tends to form behind the retina.
✓ Correction → Convex/converging lens.

◆ PRESBYOPIA
✓ Presbyopia → Age-related reduction in accommodation caused by weakening of the ciliary muscles and reduced flexibility of the eye lens.
✓ Correction → Appropriate converging lens; some people require bifocal lenses.

◆ BIFOCAL LENS
✓ Bifocal lens → Commonly combines:
Upper part → Concave lens for distant vision.
Lower part → Convex lens for near vision.

✓ Other correction methods → Include contact lenses and, in some cases, surgery.

title: 6.6 OPTICAL INSTRUMENTS
notes:
✓ Optical instruments → Use the reflecting and/or refracting properties of mirrors and lenses.

◆ EXAMPLES
Periscope • kaleidoscope • binoculars • camera • telescope • microscope.

◆ SIMPLE MICROSCOPE
✓ Simple microscope → Converging lens of short focal length used as a magnifier.
✓ Object → Placed within one focal length of the lens.
✓ Image → Erect, magnified and virtual.

◆ COMPOUND MICROSCOPE
✓ Compound microscope → Uses more than one convex lens.
✓ Objective lens → Forms an enlarged image.
✓ Eyepiece lens → Further magnifies the image.

◆ TELESCOPE
✓ Telescope → Used to observe very distant objects such as astronomical objects.
✓ Telescope → Uses optical elements to produce a magnified view of distant objects.

✓ KEY IDEA → Microscopes magnify small nearby objects; telescopes help observe distant objects.

title: 6.7 PRIMARY COLORS OF LIGHT AND HUMAN VISION
notes:
◆ PRIMARY COLORS OF LIGHT
✓ Red.
✓ Green.
✓ Blue.

✓ Additive primary colors → Different combinations can produce other colors of light.

◆ HUMAN COLOR VISION
✓ Human retina → Contains light-sensitive cells involved in vision.
✓ Cone cells → Are responsible for color vision and respond to different ranges of wavelengths.
✓ Three types of cone response → Are associated broadly with red, green and blue regions of the spectrum.

✓ KEY IDEA → Human color vision is based on the combined responses of different cone cells.

title: 6.8 COLOR ADDITION OF LIGHT
notes:
✓ Color addition → Mixing of colored LIGHTS.

◆ ADDITIVE COLOR COMBINATIONS
✓ Red + Green → Yellow.
✓ Green + Blue → Cyan.
✓ Red + Blue → Magenta.
✓ Red + Green + Blue → White.

✓ Additive color combinations → Occur because light intensities are added together.

◆ APPLICATIONS
✓ Color displays and screens → Produce many colors by controlling the intensities of red, green and blue light.

✓ KEY IDEA → Additive color mixing uses RGB: red, green and blue.

title: 6.9 COLOR SUBTRACTION OF LIGHT USING FILTERS
notes:
✓ Color subtraction → Occurs when filters absorb some wavelengths of incident light and transmit others.

◆ SUBTRACTIVE PRIMARY COLORS
✓ Yellow → Mainly transmits red + green and absorbs much blue.
✓ Cyan → Mainly transmits green + blue and absorbs much red.
✓ Magenta → Mainly transmits red + blue and absorbs much green.

◆ FILTER PRINCIPLE
✓ Filter color → Depends on the color/range of wavelengths it transmits while absorbing others.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ White light → Red filter → Mainly red light transmitted.
✓ White light → Blue filter → Mainly blue light transmitted.
✓ Combining filters → Reduces the range of wavelengths transmitted.

✓ KEY IDEA → Addition combines light; subtraction removes selected wavelengths through absorption.
